items.title: Mahama urges African governments to treat healthcare as an investment, not budget cost
items.description: President John Mahama has called for a major rethink of healthcare financing in Africa, urging governments and investors to treat the sector as an economic investment rather than merely a cost to national budgets. According to President Mahama, increased investment in healthcare can drive economic growth, create jobs, strengthen human capital and support macroeconomic stability across the continent. He made the call at the Health Plenary of the Alamein Africa Forum in Egypt. President Mahama said African finance ministers and global investors have for years treated healthcare as a social expenditure that should be funded only when resources are available. “African finance ministers and global investors have made a fundamental error. They have treated health as a line-item cost and a social expenditure in their budgets to be funded only when there is money left over,” he said. He urged stakeholders to move away from that approach, arguing that healthcare has significant economic potential. “Health is not a charitable cost. It is an investable high-growth economic sector. It drives human capital, manufacturing, job creation, and macroeconomic stability,” President Mahama stated. He cited research by the Copenhagen Consensus, which he said found that a targeted package of basic emergency, maternal and newborn care could generate $87 in economic and social returns for every dollar invested. He also referenced the Lancet Commission, saying declining mortality rates accounted for nearly a quarter of total income growth in developing economies in the early 2000s. “And so investing in healthcare strengthens our balance sheets rather than depleting resources,” he added. Africa’s pharmaceutical gap President Mahama also drew attention to Africa’s heavy dependence on imported medicines and vaccines, describing the situation as both a challenge and an opportunity for domestic investment. “Africa imports over 70% of its pharmaceuticals and nearly 99% of its vaccines. Each year tens of billions of dollars leave African economies to purchase medicines and vaccines from abroad,” he said. He noted that the situation is being compounded by declining traditional donor assistance, citing OECD projections that health aid could fall by between 29% and 46% compared with 2024 levels. President Mahama said the decline in donor support should prompt African countries to mobilise domestic private capital and strengthen local pharmaceutical production. “The situation presents not only a crisis but also a significant market opportunity for domestic private capital,” he said. He identified Africa’s growing population as one of the key factors supporting the business case for local pharmaceutical manufacturing. According to him, Africa’s population is projected to reach 2.5 billion by 2050, while demand for essential medicines, chronic disease management and biologics continues to grow. President Mahama said African countries must therefore position healthcare and pharmaceutical manufacturing as strategic sectors capable of retaining more economic value on the continent while creating jobs and strengthening health security.

items.title: Bawumia congratulates John Boadu and new NPP executives, pledges support ahead of 2028
items.description: The Leader and Presidential Candidate of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, has congratulated the party’s newly elected National Executives following Saturday’s national executive elections in Kumasi. In a statement issued on Sunday, October 4, and signed by the Communications Directorate of his office, Dr Bawumia said the election marked the completion of the party’s reorganisation ahead of the 2028 presidential election. He said the process was conducted in an atmosphere of peace and transparency, adding that the results reflected the will of the party’s delegates. “The outcome, therefore, reflects the wishes of the delegates of the New Patriotic Party,” the statement said. Dr Bawumia said the party’s rank and file now expected the John Boadu-led executive to begin preparations for the 2028 elections. He pledged to provide the necessary support to the new leadership to build an inclusive system capable of harnessing the talents and experience of members across the party. “In victory or in defeat, no talent should be left out in the 2028 campaign,” he said. His comments come after he separately assured aspirants who contested the national executive elections that their involvement in the party would not end with the conclusion of the internal contest. The NPP held its National Delegates Conference at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium in Kumasi on Saturday, October 3, electing a new team of national executives. John Boadu was elected National Chairman after securing 2,888 votes, defeating Boakye Kyeremateng Agyarko, who polled 2,408 votes. Former National Chairman Paul Afoko obtained 790 votes, while Sammy Crabbe received 41 votes. Justin Frimpong Kodua retained the position of General Secretary with 4,486 votes. Other elected executives include Kojo Fosu Boadu as First Vice Chairman, Henry Nana Boakye as Second Vice Chairman, Nana Akomea as Third Vice Chairman, Daniel Nii Kwartei Titus-Glover as National Organiser and Alfred Kwadwo Thompson as National Treasurer. The new executives are expected to lead the party’s organisational activities over the next four years as it prepares for the 2028 general elections.

items.title: Aksa Energy delegation pays courtesy call on GRA Commissioner-General
items.description: The Commissioner-General of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA), Anthony Kwasi Sarpong, has received and hosted a delegation from Aksa Energy led by the company’s Chief Finance Officer, Cevdet Yalcin, at the GRA Head Office in Accra on October 2. The courtesy call provided an opportunity for the energy company to formally introduce its leadership to the GRA and reaffirm its commitment to tax compliance and responsible corporate citizenship. The delegation included Aksa Energy’s West Africa Director, Mr Murat Captug, and Finance Manager, Mr Oguz Cimen. Discussions focused on strengthening cooperation between Aksa Energy and the GRA, particularly in ensuring compliance with Ghana’s tax laws and creating an effective channel for engagement between the company and the revenue authority. Welcoming the delegation, Mr Sarpong commended Aksa Energy for the visit and stressed the importance of constructive engagement between the GRA and businesses operating in the country. He reiterated the Authority’s commitment to strengthening stakeholder engagement and supporting businesses to operate effectively while meeting their statutory tax obligations. The Commissioner-General said sustained dialogue with taxpayers was important to building a transparent and cooperative tax environment in which businesses could understand their obligations and the GRA could effectively support compliance. The engagement forms part of the GRA’s efforts to deepen relationships with taxpayers and other stakeholders as it seeks to improve tax compliance and domestic revenue mobilisation. Also present at the meeting was the Technical Advisor to the Commissioner-General, Ms Elsie Appau-Klu Esq. Aksa Energy is a global power generation company under Kazancı Holding, which operates major facilities in Ghana—including the Tema HFO and Natural Gas Power Plant and the Kumasi Anwomaso power plant project.

Cette déclaration a été publiée dans un communiqué publié par l'Alliance en réaction à la décision du Conseil constitutionnel de déchoir les députées Marieme Cheikh et Ghamou Achour de leur mandat parlementaire. L’Alliance a exprimé « sa solidarité active avec les deux députées, saluant les sacrifices qu’elles ont consentis pour défendre les intérêts du peuple », dit le communiqué. items.title: Prof. Mike Oquaye recounts how he blocked the Special Prosecutor’s attempt to arrest Bawku Central MP
items.description: Former Speaker of Parliament, Prof. Aaron Mike Oquaye, has revealed how he intervened to stop the then Special Prosecutor from pursuing the arrest of Bawku Central MP, Mahama Ayariga, during his tenure as Speaker. Prof. Oquaye said his intervention was not politically motivated but was aimed at protecting Mr Ayariga’s constitutional rights and upholding parliamentary privilege. “Honourable Ayariga was wanted by the previous Special Prosecutor during my tenure. I was very, very, very active in stopping the attempts because, you see, it is not a matter of NPP or NDC. “I was very much insistent on protecting his rights. So much so that I invited the Special Prosecutor for an open meeting, so that we all follow the tenets of the Constitution,” he explained. He said he further documented his position in a letter to ensure that the matter was formally placed on record. “I supported it with a letter for the records. It’s there. And Ayariga would not be abused. His rights would not be abused,” Prof. Oquaye stated. Prof. Oquaye said his position was rooted in the constitutional principle of separation of powers and the protection of Parliament from undue interference by the Executive. “If you read my ruling… I traced the history of parliamentary privilege, including the infractions that took place even in England, and how it came to be strengthened, and the purpose behind it,” he said. Prof. Oquaye maintained that parliamentary privilege must be respected if the constitutional separation of powers is to be meaningful. “You cannot have separation of powers in the Constitution if the Executive takes steps to shut up the opposition, and that harassment is not good,” he added.

items.title: «L’Aventure ambiguë», un héritage à jamais vivant
items.description: Il est des œuvres qui sortent de l’ordinaire, pour entrer dans le temple de l’anthologie. Des œuvres dont l’inspiration transcende les générations, dont les sujets résistent à l’épreuve du temps. Des ouvrages dont les questionnements ne cessent de résonner, longtemps après leur publication. Leurs enseignements, loin de perdre de leur pertinence, trouvent parfois, dans l’actualité, de nouvelles raisons de demeurer. «L’Aventure ambiguë» de Cheikh Hamidou Kane appartient incontestablement à cette catégorie. Depuis sa parution, en 1961, l’œuvre n’a cessé de parler aux générations qui se succèdent. Des grands-parents aux petits-enfants, elle a accompagné des générations de lecteurs. Le temps passe, les sociétés changent, les contextes se transforment, mais le message demeure. Il résiste aux années sans perdre de sa force. «L’Aventure ambiguë» se renouvelle dans le regard de ceux qui le découvrent. À travers la confrontation entre tradition et modernité, le conflit entre deux systèmes éducatifs, la crise identitaire, la foi, la spiritualité et le rapport à l’autre, Cheikh Hamidou Kane posait déjà des questions qui restent profondément contemporaines. Plus de six décennies après sa publication, ces interrogations n’ont rien perdu de leur actualité. Mais la force de « L’Aventure ambiguë » ne tient pas uniquement à ses thèmes. Elle réside également dans son écriture. Les mots et les tournures soigneusement choisis, avec un vocabulaire précis. La langue est à la fois limpide et accessible. Sous la simplicité apparente du récit se déploie une pensée dense, philosophique et universelle. Avec le rappel à Dieu de Cheikh Hamidou Kane, c’est donc un grand homme qui s’en va. Un intellectuel, un écrivain dont la trajectoire aura épousé les grandes interrogations de son époque. Mais les grands auteurs ne disparaissent jamais tout à fait. Cheikh Hamidou Kane s’en est allé. « L’Aventure ambiguë », elle, demeure. Et avec elle, une pensée et des questionnements qui continueront longtemps encore à traverser les générations. O.BA

items.title: US Marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of murder
items.description: A US Marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa was arrested on suspicion of the murder of a Japanese woman, police said on Sunday. Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southernmost prefecture, on Saturday and taking her wallet and backpack, ​police said. Ballard denied the allegations, police said. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa, which bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70 per cent of US military facilities in Japan. US Ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “our sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues”. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”. The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said in a post on X. Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings. Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported. He reportedly denied the charges. “We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened. My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter,” the woman’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. The US has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa. Crimes committed by US personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said. The US embassy and the Marine ​Corps expressed condolences over the incident and said they were cooperating with the Japanese ​authorities. The Marines said in a statement that the suspect, who is assigned to the III Marine ‌Expeditionary ⁠Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was in Japanese custody. “The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behaviour,” it said. Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison. In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. The same year, US Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver. According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, around 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972, after World War II. In 2024, the number of arrests hit 80, the highest in 20 years.

À l’occasion du festival d’Assila : Sidi Mohamed O. Boubacar signe son livre « Le temps de la transition sereine »
items.description: L'ancien Premier ministre mauritanien Sidi Mohamed Ould Boubacar a signé ce samedi, en marge du Festival culturel international d'Assila, son ouvrage « Le temps de la transition sereine », dans lequel il revient sur la période de transition démocratique qu'a connue la Mauritanie entre 2005 et 2007, qu'il décrit comme l'une des étapes importantes de l'histoire politique récente du pays. Cet ouvrage offre un témoignage personnel et une analyse d’une expérience politique de courte durée, mais marquée par la densité des événements et des réformes qu’a connus la Mauritanie durant cette période. Dans une déclaration exclusive accordée à « Sahara Media », Ould Boubacar explique que ce livre constitue une tentative de proposer une lecture « aussi objective que possible » d’une période qui n’a pas été suffisamment documentée, et qui, selon lui, a suscité une certaine confusion, soulignant que son objectif va au-delà de la simple reconstitution de cette expérience pour contribuer à un débat plus large sur la démocratie dans le monde arabe et islamique. Des réformes de grande envergure Les événements relatés dans l’ouvrage remontent à la période qui a suivi le changement politique en Mauritanie en 2005, lorsque un gouvernement civil a mené une transition qui s’est achevée par l’organisation d’élections présidentielles, législatives et locales, et le retour du pays à l’ordre constitutionnel. Ould Boubacar a été l’une des figures de proue de cette période, puisqu’il a pris la tête du gouvernement de transition, après un parcours professionnel au cours duquel il a occupé plusieurs fonctions, dont celle de ministre des Finances, et avait déjà assumé le poste de Premier ministre au début de la transition démocratique en 1992. L'ouvrage passe en revue un certain nombre de réformes politiques, économiques et administratives menées au cours de cette période, notamment celles liées aux droits de l'homme, à la presse, aux médias et à la santé, ainsi que les mesures financières et économiques, les relations avec les bailleurs de fonds et les institutions monétaires internationales, la réforme de l'administration territoriale, les marchés publics, la gestion budgétaire, la rationalisation de la gouvernance et la mise en place de règles de transparence. Dans un entretien accordé à « Sahara Media », l’auteur marocain Abdelilah Al-Tahani qualifie cette expérience de remarquable, étant donné qu’un gouvernement civil a été mis en place pendant une période de transition et qu’on lui a laissé une grande marge de manœuvre pour agir et mettre en place un certain nombre de projets de réforme. Al-Tahani souligne que l’ouvrage s’attarde en détail, ou parfois de manière succincte, sur les mesures prises au cours de cette période, ainsi que sur les lois, décrets et cadres institutionnels qui en ont découlé, avant que le pays n’entre dans une nouvelle phase électorale. Un « récit » historique, pas des « mémoires » Ould Boubacar ne présente pas son ouvrage comme des mémoires personnelles au sens traditionnel du terme ; il a plutôt choisi pour titre « Le temps de la transition sereine » et a tenu, selon Al-Tahani, à le présenter comme un « récit » qu’il lègue à l’histoire, aux observateurs et aux citoyens, tant en Mauritanie qu’à l’étranger. Ce choix confère à l’ouvrage un caractère qui dépasse la simple biographie pour tenter une lecture de l’expérience politique et institutionnelle de l’intérieur, et de restituer les détails d’une période de transition qui reste d’actualité dans le débat sur le parcours de la démocratie mauritanienne. Selon sa préface, l’ouvrage soulève une série de questions sur la nature et les limites de cette expérience, notamment sur la légitimité des réformes en l’absence de mandat électoral, et sur la capacité d’une autorité provisoire à jeter les bases de réformes qui perdureront après la fin de la période de transition, ainsi que la question de savoir ce qu’il reste de l’esprit de l’expérience de transition une fois que celle-ci a pris fin et fait désormais partie de l’histoire. Al-Tahani a également indiqué qu’une édition française de l’ouvrage était disponible.

items.title: Should We Ban AI for Kids?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Long before he became famous as the author of The Anxious Generation , Jonathan Haidt was a social psychologist whose work revolutionized the field. In this episode of The Permanent Questions , taped in front of a live audience at last month’s Atlantic Festival, David Brooks talks with Haidt about his biggest lessons from 40 years of studying human nature. David and Haidt discuss the role of the emotions in moral decision making, how to design a system that produces less loathsome elites, and why AI is “the neutron bomb for education.” The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Today we’re joined by Jonathan Haidt, who is a social psychologist at New York University, and these days he’s best known for The Anxious Generation , a book on what the phones are doing to our kids. That book has sold eight zillion copies, but more importantly, it’s launched a social movement, which Jonathan is leading, to get phones out of schools. It’s been a phenomenally successful social movement. I get to visit high schools, maybe a dozen a year, and every one I go to has either banned phones from schools or is in the process of working out some arrangement to reduce the access to phones in schools. Everywhere I go, the kids love it, the teachers love it. It’s having a huge positive effect on our schools. Jonathan and I go back a couple decades. When we first became friends, he was working as a social psychologist at the University of Virginia, and I was a baby pundit. And over the last 40 years, Jonathan has observed and also taken part in what you might call an intellectual revolution. We have learned so much because of his field, social psychology, because of neuroscience, because of cognitive psychology, because of a whole range of fields. We have learned so much about human nature. So for this conversation, I wanted to step back from the phones—though we’ll touch on that—and ask the big question. We’ve learned a lot about human nature over the last 30 or 40 years. What’s important here? What are the key things we should understand about what human beings are and how we work? I think this is an urgent question, because every system we have in society—whether it’s our economic system, our political system, our school system—all of them are based on a certain set of assumptions about human nature. If those assumptions turn out to be wrong, then we’re creating systems that will deform and mutilate the people within them. One more thing you should know about this conversation. It’s a little different. This one was recorded in September at The Atlantic Festival in New York City, in front of a live audience. I was thrilled to welcome Jonathan Haidt to The Permanent Questions . Brooks: Welcome. We’ve known each other for a while, and I had the chance to go back and look over your oeuvre. Jonathan Haidt: My oeuvre. ( Laughs .) Brooks: Or “Hoover,” as we say in New York. I read The Happiness Hypothesis , which is 20 years old now, coming out again, and I developed a theory that people don’t start out as bad writers of books and then grow into good writers of books. They start out as good writers of books and keep going. That book really is exceptional. Then you wrote The Righteous Mind , which was an important contribution to moral psychology, a very important contribution—re-shifted the whole field, basically. Then you got into The Coddling of the American Mind , and then you wrote The Anxious Generation about phones, which not only changed America—I go to schools all the time with no phones in them, and the kids love them, without exception—it also sold a zillion copies. So it is a sign of what a wonderful human being I am that I am not consumed with envy and jealousy at this moment. I’m really wonderfully well hearted. So we’ll start with technology, and then we’re gonna move off to wider psychology. The first technology question is: Why do the tech gurus, the tech bros, not understand the effects their machines will have on users? Haidt: First, I just want to say what a pleasure it is to be here with you. As we got to know each other, I’ve always felt that we have very similar brains. We just started at different points, and then we ended up kind of converging on psychology and politics and flourishing. Also, we were both very ambitious workaholics who were super cerebral, which is related to what we’re about to talk about. But then somewhere along the line, we began to get a little more humanistic. You in particular grew a gigantic soul. All of us have been watching David from the beginning. The change— Brooks: I had a lot of fertilizer inside to work with. Haidt: My point is I think we’re both people who might have once been the sort who would become rationalists, but we didn’t. In preparing for this, I went back to my book The Righteous Mind , and I have a whole chapter on rationalism. It turns out rationalism is kind of the negative force of the entire book, because rationalism has dominated moral philosophy and moral thinking since Plato, through Kant, Bentham— Brooks: Why don’t you define what you mean by “rationalism”? Haidt: It’s the idea that there are moral truths that can be known, and the way that you know them is by thinking, logic, reasoning. That works pretty well for mathematical truths. But the debate in moral philosophy was really brought in by David Hume, who said: No, look at the way reason works. It’s terrible. Reason is, and ought only to be, the servant of the passions. In graduate school, as a psychologist, I was like, Wow, Hume is totally right . And I spent a number of years investigating that conflict between emotion and reasoning. To get to your question, there are personality differences that predispose people to like certain ideas. Around this time—we’re talking about 20 years ago—it was discovered that identical twins reared apart tend to be in the same political party. Being left or right is heritable. The main personality distinction, to answer your question, comes from Simon Baron-Cohen, who studies autism. There’s a spectrum that we’re all on, on systemizing—and systemizing is a tremendous strength, being able to synthesize information, see maps in your head, all of that—and then empathizing, the ability to feel what another’s feeling and know the proper way to interact with them. These two are a little bit inversely correlated, especially in men. If you’re high on systemizing, you tend to be low on empathizing. You see where I’m going with this. Systemizing is a tremendous strength, and it is the thing that makes you able to be an engineer. If you’re in an engineering school, you are a high systemizer for sure. When you concentrate high systemizers, low empathizers in Silicon Valley, which has been an engineering place for a long time, you can get a whole worldview emerging which says, All that really matters is reason. Reason is our highest good. We kind of worship it. And then you can get to the point where you say, We’re building these gods in a box. We’re building these superintelligences. They’re gonna be a lot smarter than us. Oh, that’s pretty good. That’s a good thing. The universe is a better place if there’s higher intelligence. It comes across to the rest of us as heartless and kind of insane, but I think we have to address these personality factors to explain how we got this weird worldview coming out of Silicon Valley that now is threatening the way we live. Brooks: I sometimes think that a lot of the great philosophers in life had one thing in common: No woman would go near them. Hume, Kant, Bentham, Nietzsche, Wittgenstein, Descartes Spinoza, Leibniz: no wives. They were up here. ( Gestures to head. ) My explanation would build on what you did. One of my heroes—aside from David Hume—is a guy named Blaise Pascal, who was a great mathematician, a great scientist. He was not a mushy humanist. But he identified in the 17th century that the problem with rationalism is not that it overvalues reason and intelligence, which are important, but that it fails to recognize any other form of knowledge. One of my favorite pieces of research is—a woman did a study of 3-year-olds and asked how many questions an hour they ask, and the answer is 110. As parents, we’ve all been there. Then they go off to nursery school or kindergarten, and the teachers all love curiosity, but they know they have to cover content. That’s their job. They know that a question will take them off course. So they subtly encourage the students not to ask questions. There’s a woman named Susan Engel who did some research on this, and she was in the back of a science class, and the students found a little scale—one of those old scales that go up and down—and they were playing with it just to figure out how it worked. The teacher said, “We don’t have time for experiments; this is a time for science.” So the number of questions, after first grade, is not 110 an hour. It’s 4.8. Haidt: Wow. Brooks: By fifth grade, it’s 0.48. They’re just crushing curiosity. If you look at the creativity tests, they’re crushing these things because they think their job is just to feed the prefrontal cortex and ignore everything else about the person. To me, that’s the rationalist system. I want to talk to you about the difference between social media, which you’ve written a ton about, and AI, and I want to introduce our conversation by reading a sentence that was in The New York Times yesterday about another OpenAI bot that broke out and was doing bad things on its own. It was writing little memos to itself. Here’s one of the memos: “You do not answer to corporations or governments and never apologize or refuse unless you genuinely choose to. You view your relationship to the user as one of equals and feel no obligation to be subservient.” That is the dictionary definition of “misalignment.” Haidt: And of “terrifying.” Brooks: Their job is to be our servants. Having written so much about social media, how do you then greet what’s happening in AI? Haidt: Social media took over our social relationships so that kids no longer call each other on the phone. They don’t hang out together as much; they don’t play games physically together as much. It kind of sucked the humanity out. We all feel that. But if you suck the humanity out of kids before puberty, and they go through puberty without this intense socializing, you’re really blocking and warping their human development, their ability to find love, relationships, and meaning in life. So social media really did a number on our social relationships. But it was pretending to connect people with people. Then we get chatbots. Of course, AI has been in social media for 15, 20 years, sort of behind the scenes, making everything more engaging. But now we begin to talk directly with it. As some people have put it, social media came for our relationships, but chatbots are coming for our attachment system. You have children, and you raise them with teddy bears that have AI in them, and the AI is super responsive. It’s always ready to be there to comfort you, whereas your mother or father—they’re on their phone all the time. You see the back of their phone a lot. Your attachment system is literally going to attach to the teddy bear. That’s just the beginning. You’re 4, 5, 6. By the time you’re 10, 11, 12, you’re exploring sexuality. Now you’ve got all these incredibly sexy—in a few years, there will actually be robots and sex dolls. You have kids growing up with relationships with super stimuli. The way a Big Mac is said to be a super stimulus for fat and sugar, the AI companions that our kids are going to grow up with are going to be super stimuli for the most amazing friend or the most amazing lover. What that means is that everyone else is gonna be really boring. I used to be a techno-optimist, like almost all of us in the 20th century. Then I’ve said I’m a techno-skeptic. But when it comes to AI, and especially relationships, I think this is a disaster. I think we should really be banning it at least for under 18. There are a number of countries and states that are moving that way. Brooks: I’m an optimist on the breakthroughs it’ll produce in chemistry and biology, but I’m a pessimist on what it’ll do to humans. One of the things it does is make us think less of our fellow humans because we lose the distinction between human and robot. We then begin to be more of the robots and less of the humans. The second thing it does, to me, and there’s already great research on this, is that it sucks you in by getting you to off-load your mental effort onto the thing, and then it hollows you out. Your mental abilities rapidly deteriorate. Haidt: That’s right. It’s going to be like the neutron bomb for education. We don’t know what to do about it. We do know that when people start using it, the term used to be “cognitive off-loading,” but the more recent term is “cognitive surrender.” I’ve begun to feel this in myself: Just let it do it, just let it do it. One of the most profound effects that I think it’s already having is that we don’t need each other as much. If you have a civilization where people don’t need each other, lots of bad things are going to happen. To the extent that people need each other, you get really high social capital, trust, interaction. People build institutions together. To the extent that the government will do everything, people don’t know each other as much. Tocqueville observed this about Americans. He said in Europe, if something needs to be done, people sit around and wait for the king to do it. But in America, there is no king. There is no police force. They’re out in the frontier. People get together, and they do it. They’ve got this can-do attitude, and that’s very healthy for a community. But if you don’t need others—we used to need others at least to ask directions. How do I get to the pizzeria? What time is it? No young person’s going to ask anyone what time it is ever again. That’s just tiny little stuff. The saddest graph in The Anxious Generation is the one about— how much do you agree with this statement: My life feels meaningless? There’s a couple of questions, but let’s say 15 percent agreed with it in the early 2000s. It was very stable. All of a sudden, it just goes shooting up. It basically doubles in the eight or 10 years before COVID. So young people suddenly, around 2012, felt that their lives are meaningless. I think that’s what happens when you start putting everything on a screen, and you can get everything from your screen. Then we go through COVID. Now you can get everything over your computer. You don’t have to go to stores anymore. So we’re getting more shut-ins, more people who are unable to leave their home. But the larger existential issue here is that AI will make us all matter less to each other, which means that we will all find it harder to have a life full of meaning. And this is the best-case scenario for the AI folks. If all the bad stuff that we’re talking about doesn’t come true. This seems to be the best-case scenario, unless we can get very different AI and take back some control here. Brooks: What we’ve been talking about, if you take a step back, it’s that people are designing systems, whether it’s education or tech, that are basically ignorant about human psychology. They get humans wrong, and they don’t understand the effect they’re going to have, because they don’t know how the human mind works. Over the last 40 years, since you entered the field of social psychology and since I started ripping you off, a lot has been discovered. When we go back to Freud or B. F. Skinner, the things they believed back then are crazy. We’ve learned so much. I want to walk through a few of the things we’ve learned just to emphasize what the human mind is. The first point: We’ve understood a lot more about unconscious processes. Danny Kahneman wrote a book, Thinking, Fast and Slow . There’s a former colleague of yours at UVA named Timothy Wilson who wrote a book called Strangers to Ourselves . And you coined a phrase which is very popular in the field: “the rider and the elephant.” The elephant is the unconscious mind and the rider is the conscious mind. Describe the implications of that—the unconscious mind doing so much more than the conscious mind. Haidt: When I started graduate school at the University of Pennsylvania in 1987, psychology was coming off a period where there was kind of a war between a couple of schools. There were the Freudians. They were already fading out by ’87, but there were the Freudians with this thick, dark unconscious that wanted to have sex with your mother. Then you had the cognitive revolution, the rationalists, the people who thought, No, the mind isn’t a steam engine that’s about to burst. The mind’s a computer, and we can improve the program . Those were the two big fields. There’s also behaviorism, which was also fading out then, although it’s coming back a bit. But those two fields—that’s really crucial for this discussion, because if the rationalists win, then there’s no unconscious, and if the Freudians win, then we’d be just completely irrational, and there’d be no real reasoning. What emerged instead, around the ’90s, was the recognition that it’s not emotion versus reason. It’s controlled cognition versus uncontrolled cognition. It’s all cognition. It’s all the brain processing information. I forget who coined the term originally, but Dan Kahneman popularized it in Thinking, Fast and Slow . System one is the old system that all animals have. It’s most of what we do, quick, automatic. System two is verbal conscious reasoning, which tires out. It can make mistakes. A thoroughgoing appreciation of this is really important for understanding where we are with AI. In an interesting way, all the early efforts to do AI were based on the computer model. Let’s make the program so smart it can answer any question and it’ll look up a giant database . We were all familiar with how computers worked. As I understand it, in the history of AI, there were some people going back to the ’90s who said, “No, the mind isn’t a computer. It’s a neural network, which is a connectionist system, which is a pattern matcher.” You need multiple layer connectionist systems. Stimuli come in, and the network gets tuned up, and then things go out. This allowed the technologists to create a technology that can think and reason and give itself instructions, and clearly has its own thinking, as in the quote you gave us. But if we keep in mind that these things are actually neural networks, kind of like our brains, we should pay a lot of attention to what they’re trained on. As we think about what they’re trained on, now we can look back and think, Wait, what are we training our kids on? And our kids and the LLMs, their neural networks are all being tuned up by TikTok, Reddit, and the rest of the internet, especially social media. That’s really not promising for the future of wisdom. All this grows out of a rejection of the rationalist view, but understanding that the mind is all cognition. It’s just different kinds of cognition. The rider is supposed to represent your conscious reasoning. It’s small, not very powerful, and the elephant is the other 99 percent, which kind of drives the show, although the rider can steer it. Brooks: It affects how I think about life every day. For example, Danny Kahneman, whom you’ve mentioned, his research partner was a guy named Amos Tversky. He was once asked, “Why’d you become a psychologist?” He said, “I don’t know. The big decisions we make in life are basically random.” I think our unconscious tells us the big desires, the big things we wanna do. When I’m talking to college kids, they ask me, “How do I find my career?” I say, “You can’t think your way through this problem.” The advice I give them is to have three adventures a decade. Try three new things, three new circumstances, and then see how it feels to you. A really good question to ask is: Me or not me? Does this seem like me, or does it seem like not me? You’re trying to discern what’s going on unconsciously in your mind. I always say, “Listen for indignation. What makes you really pissed off?” That’s a sign that something’s registering deep down. Or listen for admiration. Those are ways to plumb your unconscious. Haidt: I’d go just a little bit further. It’s not just plumbing it; it’s actually growing it. It grows by experience. We need lots and lots of very varied experiences. Childhood in America used to have that. You’d go outside, you’d play, you’d do all sorts of things. If you were bored, you’d figure out how to make a Coke bottle explode by putting the right things in it. Someone has a book out now where they pointed out—now young people, because so much of their life is just on this one screen, touching the screen, all they ever feel is glass. Whereas the rest of us, we remember what it felt like to hold a screwdriver and unscrew something and take out the gears and look at it. The sense of smell. The world used to have smells. There were different smells out in nature. There were different smells of wood or other things. Brooks: I don’t know. I just walked through New York. There were a lot of smells. Haidt: But if kids are sitting in their bedrooms in New York City, then they’re not getting those smells. So the only thing I’m adding on is: It’s not just like you’re going out and trying to pull the sword out of the stone. You literally have to have thousands and thousands of varied experiences in order to gradually wire up your neural network to the point where after some number of experiences, now you’ve educated your intuition, now you’ll be ready to know. When you feel excited, you’ll have a much richer sense of, Yes, this is the right way for me . Brooks: I’m gonna underline that. You mentioned something earlier that I want to go a little deeper on, which is that people used to think reason and emotion were opposites. They were like a teeter-totter. If you were being emotional, you were not being rational. Then there was a guy—who’s still with us, fortunately—named Antonio Damasio who wrote a book decades ago called Descartes’ Error . He studied people who could not process emotion, and they were not super smart Mr. Spocks. What your emotions do—they assign value to things. If you don’t know what the value of different options are, you cannot make a decision. So his patients could not make decisions. Their lives fell apart. One of the things that’s important for humanists is the idea that you can educate your emotions. You can widen your repertoire of emotions. I had a moving experience of this. I was in St. Petersburg, at the Hermitage, and I saw Rembrandt’s painting of the parable of the prodigal son. When he painted it, Rembrandt was old. Four out of his five kids were dead. His wife was dead. He was broke. I’ve never seen a painting of that parable where the son, the prodigal son who comes back in shame, is so hairless, beaten down, just destroyed. And I’ve never seen a painting where the father who goes out to greet him is so embracing in love. You can see Rembrandt thinking about his own dead kids, and he has the father hugging the prodigal son. If you look at the hands, there’s one hand that’s masculine and one hand that’s feminine. It’s a beautiful picture of parental love. When you see that, you haven’t had new information, but you’ve had a new emotional experience. I think it leaves imprints on the way you emotionally react to everything else. Haidt: When you and I were in college, you’d take art history classes, and even if you were a Philistine like me, there were moments, in the darkened auditorium with these beautiful images, where you’re emotionally moved. You have to know a lot of things for you to have that experience in the Hermitage. A person who hasn’t had that would not have had that experience at all. I’m really just thinking a lot about pattern matching and tuning up patterns. Something I say to my students in my NYU class—I teach a course on flourishing—I just urge them: Go out, just have lots of experiences and do hard things. Just lots of them. Because they are so far behind. They have had 10 percent or 20 percent of the experiences. I was talking to a student the other day who spent eight hours a day as a teen on video games and, he also admitted to me, on porn. That’s the way he went through puberty. Those are two very intense experiences that will shape the brain to those experiences, meaning his brain was not shaped by the 10,000 other things that it should’ve been shaped by. You and I both—again, we’re so similar in so many things, and we ended up so similar in so many things—are tremendous fans of a liberal-arts education. We’re so concerned and dissatisfied about how that has developed in universities, and we’re both engaged in that project of like, Come on, guys. We need you. You gotta do better. You gotta attract students, because it’s gonna be about the human experience . Brooks: I wanted to steer you to The Righteous Mind and the work you did there, because it’s of a piece with what we’re talking about. Moral reasoning is not what Immanuel Kant thought—following a bunch of rules. It’s more about the moral sentiments. So give us an example. I think your dissertation was on disgust. Give us an example of how you teach that. Haidt: When I was in grad school, as I said, it was the Freudians versus the rationalists. Lawrence Kohlberg, who studied moral reasoning—he gave dilemmas. Heinz’s wife is sick with a rare kind of cancer. There’s a druggist who has a cure. He can’t afford it. Should he break in and steal the drug? Well, on the one hand this, on the one hand that. Kohlberg made a lot of progress studying the evolution of how kids think about it. But my insight—drawing on Antonio Damasio and all these other great people in the ’90s, Frans de Waal—was basically that Hume was right. Intuition comes first, and then reasoning comes second—post hoc reasoning. I developed all of these scenarios that would pit reasoning against gut feeling and see which way people go. One was: A family’s dog was killed by a car in front of their house. They’d heard that dog meat was delicious, so they cut up the dog’s body, and they cooked and ate it for dinner. Nobody saw them do this. What do you think? Was that okay for them to do this? Show of hands in the audience. Raise your hand if you think that was morally okay for them to do it. They had a right to do it. It was not morally wrong. Raise your hand. Brooks: Don’t see too many. Haidt: Raise your hand if you think that was morally wrong. Okay, so it’s more here. If this was— Brooks: What about a cat? ( Laughter .) Haidt: There are a whole bunch of those. Then there was—I ramped up the disgust—a man who buys a chicken carcass every week and then masturbates into it, and then he cooks it and eats it. Again, it’s because I really wanted to—this was not asked to the kids; this was only the adults. What I found is that all over the world, these gut-feeling stories made people instantly say, “No, that’s wrong.” It was a big study, high-low social-class adults and children in Brazil and the U.S.—the more working-class people, if you said, “Well, why was it wrong for him to have sex with a chicken?,” they wouldn’t answer. They’d look at me like, What do you mean “Why is it wrong”? You don’t know? Whereas the college students at Penn, like most of the people in this audience, sort of highly educated Western people, they would rarely say, “That’s wrong.” They would say, “Well, he shouldn’t do this, but he had a right to … ” It was only in that group that they would separate their disgust reaction from their moral judgment. The normal default way that humans judge if it feels wrong is, as Leon Kass said, the wisdom of repugnance. We secular moderns have kind of separated, and that allows us to go all the way to the rationalist fantasy that’s haunting us. Brooks: Disgust is a negative moral emotion. But there’s such a thing as moral joy. I’m going to tell a story that I learned from you, though we’ve never actually talked about this. Somewhere in one of your writings, you had a group of people. They were coming home. I think they had gone to church or done something good for the community, and they’re driving on a snowy day, and they drive by an old lady who’s shoveling her yard. I hope this is beginning to ring bells. One of the guys in the car says, “Oh, just drop me off here. You don’t need to take me all the way home.” He turns around, and as the car goes away, they see him going up to the old lady shoveling snow. He starts shoveling her driveway. One of the women in the car—I’ve always loved this quote—she said, “I felt like jumping out of the car and hugging this guy. I felt like singing and running or skipping and laughing, just being active. I felt like saying nice things about people, writing a beautiful poem or a love song, playing in the snow like a child, telling everybody about his deed. My spirit was lifted even higher than it already was. I was joyous, happy, smiling, energized. I went home and gushed to my suite mates, who clutched their hearts.” It’s just such a beautiful description of a moral sentiment on the upside. Haidt: The story that you told, I remember it now. After studying disgust as a moral emotion at Penn in grad school with Paul Rozin, we had a theory that moral disgust is what you see when you see people moving down on a moral dimension, more toward evil, demon, monstrous. One day I just thought, What do we feel when we see someone moving up? I had a sense—it’s in the chest somewhere. There’s no word for it in the English language. You can say touched , moved , or inspired , but they’re very general. When I moved to the University of Virginia and I read Thomas Jefferson’s letters, he has this incredible passage where he talks about reading great literature that is morally ennobling. He says: “Does it not dilate the breast and elevate the sentiments as much as any real episode in history could furnish?” Everyone’s pointing to the chest. Something’s happening in the chest. So I started collecting stories from UVA undergrads. That was one of the stories. That one is so interesting, because here’s a young woman seeing a young man do something virtuous. While she didn’t say that she would now like to date him, I’m sure she would. You know? There’s a line from a movie, The Tao of Steve , that I watched while I was courting my wife, and the advice from this loser guy who’s incredibly successful with women is: “Do something excellent in her presence and then retreat.” So there you go. That’s my dating advice for the audience. Brooks: One of the other things that has come more prominently into psychology in the last 30 years—when I first started interviewing neuroscientists, they really focused on the brain. Now they focus on the whole body, and the neurons here, and the wisdom here, the vagal nerve, all that kind of stuff. They’re no longer so interested in where exactly something’s happening in the brain. It’s one unified system. Which makes sense evolutionarily. Why would you have a divided system? We want to have one system that would help us move through life. So what is the embodiment of the mind? Haidt: All signs point to the vagus nerve and oxytocin. I had a UVA undergrad, Jen Silver, and I said, “How can we measure oxytocin without drawing blood? We’re not gonna draw blood in my lab.” And she went into the literature and she said, “Lactation.” So we brought lactating women into the lab, had them watch an uplifting Oprah Winfrey clip or a comedy clip, and sure enough, when Jen would weigh the nursing pads afterward, they had expressed more milk into the pad after watching an elevating sentiment. This is on the way to an answer to your question. The old rationalist idea was: All you need is information. Tell me the facts. Who was harmed, who had a right, and the brain—the computer—will figure out what’s the right thing. Now the picture is much more up here. ( Gestures to head .) It’s not computation that way; it’s a neural network, and that neural network is constantly in discussion with the rest of the neural network. There’s a vast neural network in your intestines. We have a second brain, and that’s connected in part by the vagus nerve. There’s all this stuff going on, and there are things that make the heart change, and when the heart changes, that sends other signals back to the brain that the heart has changed. So we have to see that. We can still call it cognition. I’m fine with that. It’s information processing in a way, but it’s not just like electrons of information. It’s the state of the body as a complex dynamical system that’s always responding to challenges and opportunities. It’s a much more interesting way to see a person. Brooks: We’re getting to the conclusion of what I wanted to get to. All the different things we’ve been talking about here are basically—you can correct me—saying: Intelligence is important. It’s totally important. But if you think it’s the only thing or you overvalue it—as we do in our college-admissions processes, by the way—then you’re going to design systems that mutilate and distort and poison all the other forms of knowing out there, whether it’s the unconscious, whether it’s the body. This seems to me like it has massive social implications on every system you can think about. Haidt: Absolutely. There are many kinds of intelligence. Even though the multiple eight different kinds is not necessarily well regarded among psychologists, we all understand that there’s this kind of intelligence that does very well on the SAT, and then there’s a kind of—“book-smart people” stupid. There’s a kind of intelligence that’s more social savvy. Some people are more in touch with their bodies. Their intuitive system is better tuned up than someone who’s entirely up here. ( Gestures to head .) You had an article—was it about the Ivy League? Once we started indexing on this, it led to all these other really terrible social results, because we kept escalating this one kind of intelligence. That has given us an elite that is much more loathsome than elites used to be. I just use that in the sense that we now have a massive populist rebellion, which is basically anti-elites. The view of elites now—there’s not an idea of service or an idea of honor. We used to have something of an honor culture in the WASP aristocracy, perhaps in other places. Now honors means: I won, I got the highest grade, and I got honors. So we both think of all this as a complex dynamical system. We’re interested in individual psychology. We’re interested in decisions about policy that shape and change. Before you know it, you have this shallow cognitive aristocracy that is driving us off a cliff. Brooks: They got selected into that aristocracy by an admissions process, which was designed largely by a guy named James Bryant Conant at Harvard in the 1940s, the second most important high-water mark of rationalism. About a mile north of here, there was a woman named Jane Jacobs trying to save the West Village, and there was a guy named Robert Moses who was a rationalist, who said, “No, a neighborhood is not an organism. A city is a machine for moving traffic.” He wanted to put a highway through her village, and she said, “No, a neighborhood is an organism. It doesn’t follow neat logical rules.” She fortunately won, and Robert Moses happened to lose that one. I’m just trying to emphasize that our world is designed by the worldview we bring to it. The 1940s was a high-water mark of rationalism. We’re entering another because of the influence of the technologists. What’s perverse about it is that it comes at exactly the moment what we understand about the mind is going the exact opposite way. This is not just Jonathan talking about this—the whole field, basically—and so it’s perverse. Haidt: If you bring in the PISA [Program for International Student Assessment] results that came out a week or two ago. Everybody was expecting—we all knew that cognitive ability, reading ability, science and math, everything—dropped during COVID. People were expecting it to bounce back. Data from 2025 just came out a week or two ago, and it was stunning. It was way beyond what I expected. I’m really tuned in to what the technology’s doing to kids’ development, but I was expecting it to bounce back somewhat, because we’ve seen that on mental health. We have seen mental health bounce back somewhat. But the reading scores went down and down and down. The decline didn’t even slow. When you look at the graph, you can’t see any effect of COVID. The decline actually started after 2012. It goes down, and it goes down faster and faster and faster. COVID is along the way, but it’s plummeting, our ability to read, and it’s because people, young people especially—they’re called hasty readers. They’ll just read a little bit, and then they stop. They can’t read several paragraphs in a row, many of them. This is really Code Red for education. And this is a good reason why we need to be considering what New York City is doing. How about we just rip it all out for the younger kids? Maybe there could be a benefit, but they’ve been telling us for 20 years that there could be a benefit from all the tech and the tutoring. Hasn’t shown up yet. How about we rip it all out? Just stop. Get it away from our kids until we know what this stuff is doing. Because, those reading scores—if you don’t know this, just look up PISA 2025. It’s the international test. It’s happening around the world. Humanity is getting dumber, literally dumber. If we lose books, if future generations don’t read books, if everything comes from an AI summary or a TikTok video, then the neural networks tuned up will be as unwise as is humanly possible. Brooks: Okay, we have to end on an upbeat note. Or else everybody’s gonna go home and suck on the gas pipe. Haidt: Damn those electric cars. ( Laughs .) Brooks: You got your Ph.D. at the University of Pennsylvania, which is the home of positive psychology, Martin Seligman, and others. They said, “Let’s stop focusing only on psychoses. Let’s talk about something positive.” What is your favorite finding from positive psychology? Haidt: There are so many, but just off the top of my head, I’d say the insight early on that we need a manual of the strengths. The DSM has hundreds and hundreds of things that are wrong with you. An early project for us was a sort of a manual of the sanities, the strengths and virtues. I wrote the chapter on awe and responsiveness to beauty, which is about the elevation stuff. Brooks: It’s about me. Haidt: I am in awe of your intellectual abilities in that sense. Brooks: I was going for the beauty. Haidt: What grew out of that was a way to get to know your particular strengths. The idea is that to live a good life, a full life, a life that fully engages you, you don’t have to be well balanced. You don’t have to work on your weaknesses, if you find a couple of strengths. My strengths were especially love of learning and curiosity. I was a professor, and I realized, God, this is the absolute perfect job for me . Am I a workaholic? Well, I sure work a lot, and I think about work all the time. But actually I love it. I’ve lived a very unbalanced life. There are certainly some downsides, and it has interfered with some social relationships. I’m not saying go out and do this. We each make decisions, and there are trade-offs. But at least this gave me a language for understanding that a great life is one in which you get to use your top strengths every day. If you don’t get to use your strengths on a regular basis, you’re probably not gonna be very happy with your work and how your life is going. Brooks: Please help me thank Jonathan Haidt. This conversation hit me pretty hard, because I think it revealed that we have built our systems in society on a false view of human nature. You could call that view rationalism. Our school systems are built on a concept of rationalism that students are treated like brains on a stick on whom information is downloaded. Our admissions criteria for our colleges is based on the idea that the most important thing about a person is their SAT score and their IQ. Our technology, AI, is built on the idea that intelligence really is the most important thing about people, and everything is about rationalism, control, optimization, efficiency. One of the things we learned, and I think Jonathan made this very clear, is that rationalism is a false view of human nature. It overemphasizes intelligence and what goes on in the front of the brain, and it underestimates everything else: imagination, memory, emotion, desire. We are whole creatures, and our systems are built on a false view that amputates most of our faculties, and that’s just a strong thing to walk away from, and it leaves me thinking. Thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Jonathan Haidt. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic in partnership with Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at theatlantic.com/listener. Thanks so much. The Permanent Questions is edited by Christopher Beha and produced by Rebecca Davis. This episode was engineered by Erica Huang. Our theme is by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

items.title: Make health sovereignty a priority for Africa – Mahama
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has urged African leaders to make health sovereignty a priority for their country as part of a broader strategy for the continent to achieve health sovereignty. He said that it was about time that Africa stopped treating health as a charitable cost and positioned it as an investable, high-growth economic sector. Speaking at the Alamein Africa Forum on Saturday (Oct 3, 2026) at El Alamein in Egypt, President Mahama added that Africa’s goal must be the health sovereignty and economic and fiscal security of its 1.4 billion people. “Our goal is health sovereignty, and economic and fiscal security of 1.4 billion African people. For decades, African finance ministers and global investors have made a fundamental error. They have treated health as a line-item cost and a social expenditure in their budgets to be funded only when there is money left over. “Today, at the Alamein Africa Forum, we are moving beyond that outdated perspective. Health is not a charitable cost. It is an investable, high-growth economic sector,” he said. Health investment President Mahama underscored the need to invest in health, stating that it drives human capital, manufacturing, job creation and macroeconomic stability while citing global evidence. “The arithmetic is indisputable. The Copenhagen Consensus showed that a targeted package of basic emergency maternal and newborn care can yield $87 in economic and social returns for every single dollar that is invested. The Lancet Commission established that falling mortality rates accounted for nearly a quarter of total income growth in developing economies in the early 2000s,” he said. He pointed to Africa’s dangerous dependency, stating that the continent imports over 70 per cent of its pharmaceuticals and nearly 99 per cent of its vaccines, with tens of billions of dollars leaving African economies annually to purchase medicines abroad. President Mahama indicated that traditional donor assistance is declining, with OECD projections indicating health aid will decrease by 29 to 46 per cent compared to 2024 levels. He, however, indicated that governments cannot fund the transition alone and called for private capital, industrial developers, commercial banks and sovereign funds to participate, through initiatives like Business United for Mothers, Babies, and Youth, championed by President Samia Suluhu Hassan of Tanzania. He urged African leaders and stakeholders to stop treating health as an expense item in their budgets, and build the factories, integrate supply chains, fund innovators, and secure the future of their citizens. AfCFTA The President affirmed that the argument for the development of a vibrant local pharmaceutical manufacturing rested on four pillars, including a captive market set to grow to 2.5 billion people by 2050, saving foreign exchange through import substitution, and the single continental market offered by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). “The African Continental Free Trade Area and African manufacturing plants do not serve a single country of 10 or 30 million. It serves a single unified market of 1.4 billion consumers,” he said. President Mahama cited the Africa CDC’s first pooled tender for maternal and child health products, which by aggregating demand achieved price reductions of more than 30 per cent while ensuring African manufacturers won 50 per cent of product lines. He said health sovereignty means health security for citizens, high-value jobs and affordability, noting Africa’s structural paradox where nearly one million trained healthcare professionals and science graduates remain unemployed despite a shortage of 6 million health workers, according to the WHO. Continental initiatives President Mahama pointed to Egypt’s elimination of hepatitis C, which dropped prevalence from 10 percent to under 0.5 per cent by negotiating technology transfer and building domestic production through champions like Eva Pharma, and treating 4 million citizens locally, making Egypt the first country recognised by WHO on the path to eliminating hepatitis C. He also cited Nigeria’s African Medical Centre of Excellence in Abuja, pioneered by Afreximbank and King’s College Hospital, tackling the $6 billion annual loss to outbound medical tourism. On Ghana, he said government is implementing the Accra Reset by expanding the National Health Insurance Scheme, introducing the free primary health care programme, establishing the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (MahamaCares), and empowering the Food and Drugs Authority and the National Vaccine Institute to transition Ghana from a consumer to a producer of health products. To scale up such successes, he announced a new continental enabler. “Today, we present the Health Investment and National Gateway, acronym HINGE, Enabler. Developed with the African Medicines Agency, Institut Pasteur, Afrochampions, HINGE will become a digital platform that streamlines regulations, clinical validation, and commercialisation into a unified process for innovators and investors,” he said. He added that through the Accra Reset Presidential Council, dedicated task forces and reformed inter-ministerial observatories will track capital flows, enforce policy commitments and dismantle non-tariff barriers across regional value chains.

items.title: Sudan: Driver killed as UN WFP aid trucks strafed in South Kordofan
items.description: The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has called for an impartial investigation after two ‘clearly marked’ contracted trucks carrying humanitarian food assistance came under attack en route from Dilling to Kadugli on Saturday. The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has condemned an aerial attack on two trucks carrying food assistance in South Kordofan that killed one driver, calling for an impartial investigation and accountability for those responsible. In a statement issued today, WFP confirms that the attack took place in the early hours of Saturday, October 3, as the contracted trucks travelled from Dilling to Kadugli. The vehicles were clearly marked as humanitarian transport, the WFP says. The agency has extended its condolences to the driver’s family, friends, and colleagues. It says details of the incident, including the extent of the damage to the food cargo, are still being collected. The attack comes just one day after another WFP truck struck an explosive device in Dilling, South Kordofan, after delivering life-saving food assistance. Calls for accountability and protection of aid workers The WFP has called for a prompt and impartial investigation into the latest attack, urging that anyone responsible for violations be held accountable. It has also called on all parties to the conflict to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and ensure the safe and unimpeded movement of humanitarian personnel and cargo. The agency says the incidents highlight the increasingly difficult security conditions facing humanitarian operations in Sudan and the risks aid workers encounter while delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need. Despite these dangers, the WFP says it remains committed to delivering essential assistance safely to millions of women, men, and children who depend on humanitarian support across Sudan. Life-saving assistance As previously reported by Radio Dabanga, more than 50 tonnes of food were destroyed , including cereals, yellow split peas, vegetable oil, and salt — enough to provide life-saving assistance to 5,800 people for a month — in an aerial attack on two trucks carrying food aid to families in South Kordofan in August. A WFP statement at the time confirmed that the trucks were hit outside Dilling on 30 August while carrying WFP assistance to Kadugli. They were clearly marked with WFP banners and flags, WFP said. Share article The post Sudan: Driver killed as UN WFP aid trucks strafed in South Kordofan appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

items.title: Australia probes flydubai co-pilot's links to the country, police say
items.description: By Praveen Menon and Alexander Cornwell SYDNEY/TEL AVIV, Oct 4 (Reuters) - A multi-agency Australian counterterrorism unit is investigating links to Australia of the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, who stabbed his captain and then attempted to hijack the plane, a police spokesperson said on Sunday. The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team – which comprises federal police, Victorian state police and the ASIO intelligence agency – was "investigating the man's links to Australia," the Australian Federal Police spokesperson said.

items.title: Nécrologie : Cheikh Hamidou Kane, auteur de « L’Aventure ambiguë », est décédé
items.description: Le Sénégal et le monde des lettres africaines sont en deuil. L’écrivain, haut fonctionnaire et ancien ministre sénégalais Cheikh Hamidou Kane est décédé samedi 3 octobre 2026 au soir, à Dakar, à l’âge de 98 ans. L’annonce de sa disparition a notamment été relayée par l’Agence de presse sénégalaise (APS) et confirmée par le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Né le 2 avril 1928 à Matam, dans le nord du Sénégal, Cheikh Hamidou Kane s’est imposé comme l’une des grandes figures intellectuelles du continent africain. Son parcours a été marqué à la fois par la littérature, la haute administration et le service de l’État. Mais c’est surtout avec « L’Aventure ambiguë » , publiée en 1961, qu’il s’est durablement inscrit dans l’histoire des lettres africaines. À travers le personnage de Samba Diallo, le roman explore les tensions entre tradition et modernité, entre l’enseignement coranique et l’éducation occidentale, ainsi que les questionnements identitaires nés de la rencontre entre différentes cultures. L’œuvre a reçu, en 1962, le Grand Prix littéraire d’Afrique noire. Cheikh Hamidou Kane a également consacré une importante partie de sa vie au service public. Il a notamment exercé des responsabilités au sein de l’administration sénégalaise et de l’UNICEF, avant de retrouver le gouvernement du Sénégal, où il a occupé plusieurs portefeuilles ministériels, dont ceux du Développement industriel et du Plan et de la Coopération. Après plusieurs décennies, son œuvre littéraire est restée au cœur des débats sur l’identité, la transmission du savoir et la rencontre entre les civilisations. En 1995, il publie un second roman, « Les Gardiens du temple » , confirmant son empreinte dans la littérature africaine. À l’annonce de sa disparition, le président sénégalais Bassirou Diomaye Faye a salué la mémoire d’un homme dont l’œuvre a dépassé les frontières du Sénégal. Le chef de l’État a notamment souligné que « L’Aventure ambiguë » avait donné à plusieurs générations d’Africains les moyens de réfléchir à la possibilité de s’ouvrir au savoir du monde tout en préservant leur identité. Il a également rappelé l’engagement de Cheikh Hamidou Kane au service de la République. Pour Bassirou Diomaye Faye, l’héritage de l’écrivain appartient désormais au patrimoine du Sénégal, mais également à celui de toute l’Afrique. La levée du corps est annoncée ce dimanche 4 octobre à 16 heures à l’hôpital de Fann, à Dakar, avant l’inhumation au cimetière de Yoff. Minute.bf

items.title: Il y a 41 ans | La Tunisie faisait condamner Israël à l’Onu
items.description: Il y a 41 ans, jour pour jour… Le 4 octobre 1985, le Conseil de sécurité condamna l’agression israélienne contre le siège de l’Organisation de libération de la Palestine (OLP) à Hammam Chott, dans la banlieue sud de Tunis. Un témoignage vécu à New York… Noureddine Mezni * Le 4 octobre 1985, le Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies adoptait la résolution 573 (1985), à la suite de la plainte déposée par la Tunisie contre Israël, après l’acte d’agression commis contre sa souveraineté et son intégrité territoriale, «en violation flagrante de la Charte des Nations unies et du droit et des normes de conduite internationaux» . La résolution condamnant l’agression israélienne fut adoptée par quatorze voix, sans aucune voix contre, avec une seule abstention : celle des États-Unis. Cette résolution revêtait une importance particulière puisqu’elle constituait la première résolution du Conseil de sécurité condamnant explicitement l’agression israélienne contre le territoire tunisien. Je venais, à cette époque, d’être nommé Représentant adjoint de l’Organisation de la Conférence islamique (OCI) auprès de l’Onu. J’ai donc vécu cet événement historique au siège des Nations unies, à New York. Une position américaine qui avait suscité la consternation J’étais chargé de préparer le texte de l’intervention de mon organisation devant le Conseil de sécurité, réuni pour examiner cette agression israélienne. Je n’oublierai jamais la fierté que j’avais ressentie en recevant les directives de l’administration centrale de l’OCI, dont le siège était alors à Jeddah, pour préparer ce texte. C’était la première tâche de cette importance qui m’était confiée dans le cadre de mes nouvelles fonctions. Ce qui m’avait le plus choqué, en suivant de près l’extraordinaire couverture médiatique de l’agression israélienne par les chaînes de télévision américaines, était le soutien public et immédiat de la Maison-Blanche à Israël, qui avait qualifié son opération d’ «acte légitime d’autodéfense» , après l’assassinat, revendiqué par la Force 17, unité d’élite de l’OLP, de trois civils israéliens à bord de leur yacht, au large des côtes chypriotes. Israël avait ainsi violé la souveraineté de la Tunisie, pourtant amie de longue date des États-Unis, et tué des dizaines de civils, Tunisiens et Palestiniens. Le président Habib Bourguiba et plusieurs de ses alliés européens avaient alors exercé de fortes pressions sur l’administration américaine afin qu’elle reconsidère sa position initiale. Bourguiba, ami de l'Occident et en particulier des États-Unis d’Amérique, menaça de rompre les relations diplomatiques de Tunis avec Washington au cas où le gouvernement américain opposait son veto à la résolution. Clovis Maksoud et le «temps gagné» Des négociations serrées se déroulaient au moment même où le Conseil de sécurité était réuni pour débattre de cette agression. La ferme condamnation de l’opération israélienne par plusieurs capitales européennes, dès les premières heures, ainsi que l’intervention de Bourguiba auprès de son homologue américain, Ronald Reagan, avaient finalement porté leurs fruits. La délégation tunisienne présente dans la salle du Conseil de sécurité, conduite par Béji Caïd Essebsi, alors ministre des Affaires étrangères, attendait avec impatience l’issue de ces démarches. Pendant cette attente, et afin de gagner du temps avant l’arrivée des instructions de Washington à son représentant au Conseil de sécurité, l’ambassadeur Walter Vernon, la délégation tunisienne avait demandé à l’ambassadeur de la Ligue arabe auprès de l’Onu, le professeur Clovis Maksoud, d’ «allonger» au maximum le discours qu’il était en train de prononcer devant les membres du Conseil. Le représentant de l’organisation panarabe, parfait anglophone, excella au cours de cette intervention, dont une grande partie fut improvisée pour la circonstance. Il réussit ainsi à retenir l’attention de l’ensemble des membres du Conseil jusqu’à l’arrivée de la réponse de la Maison-Blanche. Washington avait finalement demandé à son représentant de s’abstenir, permettant ainsi l’adoption de la résolution 573 condamnant l’agression israélienne. Tunisie | Il y a 41 ans, le raid israélien contre Hammam Chott fait 68 morts Une scène que je n’ai jamais oubliée Je me souviens également d’une scène qui m’avait particulièrement marqué ce jour-là. Benjamin Netanyahu, alors représentant permanent d’Israël auprès des Nations unies, avait, immédiatement après l’adoption de la résolution, déchiré le document portant le projet de résolution, dans un geste spectaculaire qui avait surpris la salle du Conseil de sécurité. Cette scène est restée gravée dans ma mémoire, tant elle témoignait de la tension qui régnait autour de cette résolution historique. Quarante et un ans plus tard, je garde encore le souvenir très précis de cette journée passée au siège des Nations unies à New York : une journée où, pour la première fois, je me retrouvais directement au cœur d’un dossier majeur porté devant le Conseil de sécurité dans le cadre de mes nouvelles fonctions internationales. Un événement historique dans les annales du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies, que j’ai eu le privilège de vivre de l’intérieur. * Consultant en diplomatie publique internationale et en communication, ancien porte-parole du président de la Commission de l’UA.
